summary: This note is a clipped Wikipedia-style overview of the concept of God across philosophy, theology and religion. It covers scientific and non-theist views (Hawking and Mlodinow, Nikoletseas, Charles Bradlaugh, Stephen Jay Gould's NOMA), the attributes theologians ascribe to God, and the many names for God in Atenism, Judaism, Christianity, Islam, Hinduism, Bahá'í Faith, Sikhism and Zoroastrianism. It closes by contrasting theism, deism, pantheism, monotheism, atheism and agnosticism.
one_line: Overview of the concept of God, covering its attributes, names across religions, non-theist views, and philosophical positions such as theism, deism and pantheism.
key_facts: Stephen Hawking and Leonard Mlodinow state in their book The Grand Design that it is reasonable to ask who or what created the universe.
Hawking and Mlodinow claim questions about the origin of the universe can be answered purely within science, without invoking divine beings.
Neuroscientist Michael Nikoletseas proposed that questions of the existence of God are no different from questions of natural sciences.
In monotheism and henotheism, God is conceived of as the Supreme Being and principal object of faith.
Theologians commonly attribute to God omniscience, omnipotence, omnipresence, omnibenevolence, divine simplicity, and eternal and necessary existence.
In Atenism, possibly the earliest recorded monotheistic religion, the deity was called Aten.
In the Christian doctrine of the Trinity, God, consubstantial in three persons, is called the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.
In Islam, the name Allah is used, while Muslims also have a multitude of titular names for God.
In Hinduism, Brahman is often considered a monistic deity.
The nineteenth-century English atheist Charles Bradlaugh refused to say "There is no God" because "the word 'God' is to me a sound conveying no clear or distinct affirmation".
Stephen Jay Gould proposed an approach dividing philosophy into what he called "non-overlapping magisteria" (NOMA).
In theism, God is the creator and sustainer of the universe, while in deism God is the creator but not the sustainer.
In pantheism, God is the universe itself.
In agnosticism, God is deemed unknown or unknowable.
Because God is conceived as incorporeal, God cannot (some say should not) be portrayed in a literal visual image.
